question: Do the three repeatedly evolving capitulum components map to one common ecological cause or to distinct ecological filtering domains?

one_common_driver.prediction: orientation, phyllary posture and stickiness should be explainable by the same dominant ecological domain and should not require mutually distinct mechanism classes
one_common_driver.reason: orientation has focal transition-level present-niche evidence and a direct Asteraceae abiotic-protection manipulation; phyllary close analogs support mechanical antagonist exclusion without a pollinator-visitation gain; stickiness shows direct within-Cirsium context-dependent arthropod effects plus a cost term. The focal histories also differ in relative evolutionary depth and do not share robust transition localization.
one_common_driver.boundary: different evidence domains do not prove independent genes, developmental modules or separate selective histories for every transition

trait_specific_ecological_filters.prediction: each component can regulate a different interface between the reproductive head and its environment, allowing different histories and different selective domains
trait_specific_ecological_filters.boundary: orientation has the strongest focal ecological support; phyllary and stickiness remain mechanism-domain assignments rather than focal East-Asian adaptation proofs

orientation.physical_interface: capitulum angle controls exposure of pollen/stigma/florets to precipitation, wetting and radiation; thermal/pollinator pathways remain secondary alternatives

focal_evidence.history: 4-6 minimum changes across UFBoot; intermediate relative-depth profile
focal_evidence.present_transition_regime: U-to-D tracks BIO15-up plus BIO1-down; strict exact rank 4/126; bidirectional floor rank 3/126; combined geography-residual plus internal-edge stress 3/126
focal_evidence.origin_boundary: same current regime matches only 99/376 historical chronology-by-region scenarios

external_direct_manipulation.result: artificially erect capitula produced fewer achenes; water and UV-B reduced pollen viability; no pollinator preference between erect and nodding treatments; no meaningful orientation-driven internal thermal difference
external_direct_manipulation.reading: abiotic protection is more directly supported than pollinator attraction in this Asteraceae analog

phyllary_posture.physical_interface: appressed/spreading/recurved involucral architecture changes mechanical access to the reproductive head and can impose antagonist exclusion versus legitimate-visitor handling tradeoffs

focal_evidence.history: exactly 3 minimum changes; deepest-permissive profile; JPN36 appressed state forced on the ML terminal edge and in 0.728 of UFBoot trees
focal_evidence.broad_spatial_test: current public state-diverse panel does not show broad spatial segregation; p=0.4998 with n=4

external_direct_manipulations.result: involucral-spine removal removed deterrence of illegitimate Lepidoptera and reduced filled seeds by 22%; legitimate bee/fly visitation frequency did not increase, though visit duration increased
draining protective cupulate bracts increased seed predation in 5/6 populations and reduced final seed set without detectable legitimate-pollinator discrimination

stickiness.physical_interface: sticky involucral exudates selectively deter, trap or alter access of some arthropod guilds while other seed predators and pollinators may avoid or bypass the adhesive zone; secretion/resistance can carry production costs

focal_evidence.history: exactly 5 minimum changes; shallow relative-depth envelope 0.937-0.954; JPN06 terminal forced fraction 0.995; sticky JPN15 and nonsticky JPN06 are 100/100 ML sisters
focal_evidence.broad_spatial_test: balanced 6 sticky/6 nonsticky public occurrence panel shows no simple broad spatial segregation; p=0.1306

direct_Cirsium_evidence.result: occluding sticky bracteal exudate increased seed predation in C. discolor in Illinois in 1980, but had no effect in C. flodmani in Minnesota in 1980 or 1982
later neutralization tests in C. discolor did not increase seed predators or reduce seed production
pollinators did not contact traps; several seed predators bypassed them; ants and aphids were deterred and some predatory arthropods used the sticky inflorescences

stickiness.external_cost_benefit_context: Bejaria floral stickiness supplies a direct benefit context, whereas Datura glandular stickiness supplies substantial reproductive/demographic cost contexts

biological_synthesis: The three capitulum components are best treated as different environmental interfaces rather than one syndrome responding to one driver: orientation filters abiotic reproductive exposure, phyllary architecture filters mechanical access to the reproductive head, and stickiness filters arthropod-community access under a defence-cost tradeoff. Their unequal evolutionary depths and non-shared transition localization are therefore biologically compatible with trait-specific selection mosaics, but only orientation currently has a focal East-Asian ecological transition test.

falsifiers.orientation: direct focal Cirsium manipulation showing no wetting/radiation/pollen or fitness effect while an alternative pathway explains the transition-regime pattern
falsifiers.phyllary: JPN36 reversible phyllary manipulation showing no enemy/access/fitness effect or a clear pollinator-access benefit opposite the current protection prior
falsifiers.stickiness: within-JPN15 neutralization showing a stable context-independent sign unrelated to local antagonist community/cost, or population-replicated results inconsistent with the predicted benefit-null-cost variation

claim_ceiling: External analog effect sizes are not transported to East-Asian Cirsium.
Trait-specific ecological-filter assignments are mechanistic hypotheses with unequal focal support, not three demonstrated adaptations.
Different ecological interfaces do not prove genetic or developmental modularity.
Current evidence does not identify the historical selective cause of every reconstructed transition.
